cards.heading: dollars on the blockchain
cards.body: A stablecoin is a cryptocurrency designed to maintain a stable value — usually pegged 1:1 to the US dollar. They bridge traditional finance and DeFi, letting you hold dollar value without leaving the blockchain. The market is over $200 billion and growing fast.

cards.heading: how stability is achieved
cards.body: Different stablecoins use different mechanisms: holding actual dollars in bank accounts (USDC, USDT), locking up overcollateralized crypto (DAI), or using algorithms (most have failed). Each approach trades off centralization, capital efficiency, and resilience.

left.label: why stablecoins matter
items: park profits without going to fiat

cards.text: Not all stablecoins are equally safe. The mechanism behind the peg matters more than the marketing — algorithmic stablecoins have collapsed before, taking $40B+ with them.
Key takeaway: stablecoins make crypto useful for everyday transactions. They process more annual volume than Visa and Mastercard combined.

cards.heading: the big three
cards.body: USDC (Circle), USDT (Tether), and DAI (MakerDAO) make up over 90% of the stablecoin market. They look identical at first — all peg to $1 — but they're built on completely different trust models and have different risk profiles.

left.label: fiat-backed (USDC, USDT)
items: backed by real dollars in bank accounts

cards.heading: the algorithmic experiment
cards.body: Some stablecoins tried to maintain their peg using algorithms instead of real reserves. UST (Terra) was the most famous — it relied on minting and burning a sister token to balance supply. It collapsed in May 2022 in a death spiral, erasing $40B in days.

cards.text: USDC is the most used stablecoin on Base. It's natively issued by Circle (no bridging), audited monthly, and the default for most Base DeFi protocols.
Key takeaway: pick stablecoins based on backing model, not just the ticker. USDC = audited dollars. DAI = on-chain crypto. Algorithmic = avoid unless you understand the risks.

cards.heading: the redemption mechanism
cards.body: For USDC: anyone can deposit $1 with Circle and receive 1 USDC, or return 1 USDC and get $1 back. This creates a hard floor and ceiling. If USDC trades at $0.99 in the market, arbitrageurs buy it cheap and redeem for $1 profit, pushing the price back up.

cards.heading: reserves and audits
cards.body: Fiat-backed stablecoins publish reserve reports proving they hold enough dollars (or short-term US treasuries) to back every token. Circle publishes monthly attestations for USDC by Deloitte. Tether's reserves have been historically less transparent and more controversial.

cards.heading: real-world example
cards.body: MakerDAO's DAI uses a different model. To mint DAI, you lock up at least $150 of ETH per $100 of DAI created. If your ETH drops in value, you get liquidated automatically. This overcollateralization plus on-chain transparency keeps DAI close to $1.

cards.text: A stablecoin without redemption (or with delayed redemption) is just a promise. Always check: can I actually get my dollars back? How quickly?
Key takeaway: arbitrage is the invisible hand that keeps stablecoins at $1. Reserves provide the foundation, redemption creates the floor, and traders enforce the ceiling.

cards.heading: USDC's March 2023 depeg
cards.body: On March 11, 2023, Silicon Valley Bank — which held $3.3B of Circle's USDC reserves — collapsed. USDC briefly traded at $0.87 as panic set in. The peg fully recovered within 3 days when the US government backstopped depositors. Circle was ultimately fine, but holders had a scary weekend.

cards.heading: the UST death spiral
cards.body: UST (Terra) lost its peg in May 2022. Its algorithmic mechanism required burning LUNA tokens to mint UST 1:1. When UST dropped, the protocol minted billions of LUNA — flooding supply, crashing the price, and creating a feedback loop. $40B vanished in 7 days.

cards.heading: early warning signs
cards.body: Watch for: changes in reserve composition, redemption delays or pauses, deviations of more than 1% lasting more than a few hours, issuer legal troubles or hacks, or unusual social media silence. A healthy stablecoin trades within ±0.3% of its peg almost all the time.

cards.text: Diversification matters. Holding 100% of your stablecoins in one issuer is a single point of failure. Many DeFi users split between USDC, USDT, and DAI for redundancy.
Key takeaway: pegs can break. Real-money-backed stablecoins recover quickly when reserves are intact. Algorithmic ones often don't recover at all.

cards.heading: native USDC on Base
cards.body: Base has native USDC — issued directly by Circle on Base L2, not bridged from Ethereum. This means lower risk (no bridge contract to hack), instant finality, and transfer fees under $0.001. It's the default stablecoin for nearly all Base DeFi protocols.

cards.heading: what you can do with stablecoins on Base
cards.body: Lend USDC for ~5-8% APY on Aave or Moonwell. Provide liquidity in Aerodrome's USDC/ETH pool for trading fees. Use as collateral to borrow other assets. Or simply park dollar value while you research your next move — gas costs are negligible.

cards.heading: real-world example
cards.body: A typical Base user might hold $1,000 USDC, lend half on Aave at 6% APY, and use the other half for opportunistic swaps. That earns ~$30/year passively while keeping liquidity for trades. Try doing this on Ethereum L1 — gas alone would eat the yield.

cards.text: Sending $10,000 in USDC on Base costs less than a penny. The same transfer on Ethereum L1 could cost $5-20. This is why Base is winning stablecoin volume.
Key takeaway: stablecoins on Base are fast, cheap, and battle-tested. You're now ready to use the Stablecoin Peg Tracker tool to see how stable they actually are!
